hints: Fix the top and bottom rows and regard each column as a set of letters.
For a fixed strip, use a sliding column window to count intervals whose union contains every letter.
A two-stack queue can maintain a bitwise OR over the window in amortized constant time.
analogy: Each column is a bag of letters; count consecutive groups of bags whose union is complete.
example: In a 2 by 2 grid AB/BA with letters A and B, both rows, both columns and the whole grid contain both letters, so the answer is 5.
algorithm: For each top row, reset an n-element array of column masks. Extend the bottom row downward, OR-ing each new cell?s letter bit into its column mask. For each row pair, slide a window across the column masks. Maintain the window OR using a queue made from two stacks, each entry storing its stack?s cumulative OR. For each right endpoint, append its column; while the window OR has all k bits, pop its leftmost column. The number of removed columns is the number of valid left endpoints for that right endpoint; add it to the answer. Use 64-bit counts.
correctness: Every rectangle has a unique pair of top and bottom rows and a column interval. The column masks contain exactly the letters in their vertical strips. Union only gains letters as a window extends, so after removing all possible leftmost columns, every earlier start and only those starts produced a valid rectangle. The two-stack OR queue maintains the exact union.
complexity: For an n by n grid and at most 26 letters, each row pair performs O(n) amortized mask operations, giving O(n^3) time and O(n) working space beyond the grid.
